title: Temple Scroll (11Q19) — Hobah Translation
about: The Temple Scroll (11Q19) is the longest substantially preserved Dead Sea Scroll. Its roughly sixty-six columns present an idealized sanctuary, sacrifices, festivals, purity regulations, and laws for Israel, often recasting Pentateuchal law in a first-person divine voice. Two additional copies or related witnesses are known. Large portions are damaged, and the composition is likely layered.

translation.status: Hobah provisional source-language reading translation of major substantially preserved 11Q19 passages
translation.base_text: The Hebrew manuscript 11Q19, using its standard column sequence and publicly accessible manuscript evidence
translation.method: Fresh modern-English rendering from the Hebrew sense of representative continuous passages. This is not yet a complete line-by-line translation of all sixty-six columns. Repeated legal material is translated according to the scroll's wording rather than silently replaced with a biblical translation.
translation.confidence: Medium-high in continuous columns; medium or lower where the scroll is damaged, reconstructed, or textually difficult
translation.notes: The selection preserves the scroll's distinctive temple plan, festival calendar, purity rules, and royal law. It is explicitly labelled selected rather than falsely presented as a complete critical edition.
translation.license_note: The ancient Hebrew manuscript is public domain. Hobah English wording is newly prepared for this project.

chapters.label: Selected columns — Covenant and sanctuary
chapters.text: You shall make for me a sanctuary, and I will dwell among you. You shall keep yourselves from every unclean thing and walk according to the statutes that I command. My sanctuary shall be holy, and no impurity shall be brought into the place where I cause my name to dwell. The people, the priests, and the Levites are each given their appointed boundaries and duties.

chapters.label: Selected columns — The inner court
chapters.text: The house shall be arranged in measured order, with the holy place at its centre. Gates, chambers, courts, and passages are assigned dimensions so that the sacred precinct is separated by degrees of holiness. The altar stands in the appointed place before the house. Priests serving there must enter in purity and in the garments prescribed for their ministry.

chapters.label: Selected columns — The courts of Israel
chapters.text: Around the inner sanctuary shall be further courts for the priesthood and for Israel, each with gates according to the tribes and divisions. The plan expands the sacred area beyond the proportions of the biblical tabernacle. The arrangement expresses the scroll's concern that holiness radiate outward in ordered boundaries rather than being treated as one undifferentiated space.

chapters.label: Selected columns — Daily offerings
chapters.text: Morning and evening offerings shall be brought at their appointed times. The priests shall prepare the animals, grain, oil, and wine according to the rule and shall not alter the order of service. The altar fire and the portions assigned to God and to the priests are carefully distinguished. No defective offering is to be brought into the sanctuary.

chapters.label: Selected columns — Passover and Unleavened Bread
chapters.text: In the first month the Passover shall be kept at its appointed time. The offering is eaten within the holy boundaries prescribed for the feast, and nothing belonging to the sacred meal is treated as ordinary. For seven days the feast of Unleavened Bread follows, with its sacrifices and assemblies. The scroll gives its own detailed arrangement of offerings for the festival days.

chapters.label: Selected columns — Firstfruits of grain
chapters.text: When the first grain is ready, the offering of the firstfruits shall be presented before the Lord. From that day the counting proceeds to the next appointed feast. New grain is not treated as common before the firstfruits have been offered. The calendar orders agricultural life around sacred gifts and fixed periods.

chapters.label: Selected columns — Firstfruits of wine and oil
chapters.text: After the grain festival come appointed firstfruits for new wine and then for new oil. The scroll distinguishes these agricultural celebrations and assigns sacrifices to them. The produce of the land is received as a gift under covenant, so the first portion belongs to God before the remainder becomes ordinary food for the people.

chapters.label: Selected columns — Festival of wood offering
chapters.text: Wood for the altar is brought by appointed tribal divisions so that the fire of the sanctuary may be maintained. The offering is organized rather than left to chance. Families and tribes participate in supplying the service of the house, linking the whole people with the daily worship carried out by the priests.

chapters.label: Selected columns — Day of Atonement
chapters.text: On the day appointed for atonement the sanctuary, priesthood, and people are dealt with according to the holy rule. Work ceases, the people humble themselves, and the priestly rites address impurity and sin. The scroll emphasizes the strict holiness of the day and the separation required before those serving at the sanctuary approach sacred space.

chapters.label: Selected columns — Feast of Booths
chapters.text: At the Feast of Booths the offerings are presented through the appointed days and Israel rejoices before God. The festival closes the cycle of the year's major pilgrimage celebrations. The text orders sacrifices, assemblies, and sacred boundaries so that joy and holiness belong together.

chapters.label: Selected columns — Purity around the holy city
chapters.text: The city of the sanctuary and the land surrounding it are guarded from sources of impurity. Cemeteries, certain bodily impurities, diseased conditions, and unclean animals are assigned distances or procedures appropriate to their status. The scroll extends priestly concepts of purity into geography: the closer a place is to the sanctuary, the stricter its required holiness.

chapters.label: Selected columns — Justice and idolatry
chapters.text: Israel shall not follow other gods, make covenant with idolatry, or imitate the abominations of the nations. Witnesses and judges must examine serious accusations carefully. False testimony is condemned because it corrupts the land. Rebellion against the covenant is treated not only as private wrongdoing but as a threat to the holiness of the community.

chapters.label: Selected columns — The king
chapters.text: When Israel appoints a king, he shall be one from among his brothers. He shall not multiply horses, wives, or silver and gold for himself. A copy of the law shall remain with him, and he shall read it throughout his days so that his heart is not lifted above his brothers. His authority is therefore placed beneath the covenant rather than above it.

chapters.label: Selected columns — War and holy conduct
chapters.text: When the people go out to war, the camp shall be guarded from impurity and shameful conduct because God walks among them. Officers, priests, and fighting men each have their role, but victory is not credited simply to military power. The same holiness demanded in the sanctuary follows the covenant people into the camp.

chapters.label: Selected conclusion — A holy people in a holy land
chapters.text: The laws of the scroll repeatedly return to one purpose: Israel is to become a people ordered around the dwelling of God. Temple, calendar, agriculture, courts, kingship, purity, and war are placed within one sacred pattern. Where the manuscript breaks off or is damaged, no wording is supplied here beyond the recoverable sense.
